title: Why did my antibiotics stop working? A high school research idea
excerpt: MRSA makes an extra protein that penicillin-type drugs bind only weakly. See how chemists respond, and dock molecules into that protein with free software.
content:
"My antibiotics stopped working last winter." A course of antibiotics that does nothing is a common story. The fever stays, the cough stays, and a few days later a doctor writes a different prescription. It's easy to file that under bad luck. Chemists file it under a question they have been working on for decades: how do you build a drug that bacteria can't easily beat?

One correction before going further. A pill that did nothing isn't proof that you met a resistant infection. Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says plainly that antibiotics and antifungals do not work on viruses. A course stopped early, or an illness that was never bacterial, looks identical from the sofa. The research question survives anyway: drug-resistant bacteria are real, and you can start on part of the research this week.

## How bacteria outlast a drug that never changes

Antimicrobial resistance, in CDC's wording, happens when germs develop the ability to defeat the drugs designed to kill them. Bacteria divide quickly and their populations carry small genetic differences. When a drug kills almost every cell, a rare survivor can rebuild the whole population in its own image. The bacteria change. The molecule in your pill stays exactly the same.

CDC counts more than 9.3 million drug-resistant infections in the United States each year, and more than 39,000 deaths. A caution on that figure: CDC changed its methods for the latest update of its Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Report, and says the new numbers should not be compared directly with earlier editions.

The clearest example to study is MRSA, short for methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*. Penicillin-type drugs, called beta-lactams, work by blocking the enzymes that stitch a bacterial cell wall together, and those enzymes are known as penicillin-binding proteins. *S. aureus* strains that carry the *mecA* gene make an extra one called PBP2a. Lim and Strynadka, who published its crystal structure in 2002, spell out why: PBP2a has low affinity for beta-lactams, so it keeps building the cell wall at drug concentrations that shut down the normal penicillin-binding proteins.

![Colorized electron micrograph showing clusters of round yellow bacteria on torn red human cell membranes against a dark background](/editorial/ideas/antibiotic-stopped-working-research-idea/1.jpg "MRSA under an electron microscope, colorized. The yellow spheres are the bacteria named in the method below; the red sheets are the remains of a human white blood cell.")

## Picking a target bacteria cannot easily change

Drug research starts with a choice that sounds simple and isn't: what, exactly, should your molecule grab?

If the answer is a single bacterial protein, the bacteria have an exit. One gene codes for it, and mutations can reshape the pocket the drug was built for until the drug no longer fits. PBP2a is that escape route in finished form, a protein that does the wall-building job while binding the drug weakly, so blocking the usual enzymes is no longer enough.

So you ask a narrower question. Which parts of a bacterium are hard to change without breaking the bacterium? Enzymes have some freedom to shift shape. The building blocks those enzymes work on have less of it, because many enzymes have to recognize them.

## What the teixobactin paper actually reported

In 2015, Ling and colleagues published a paper in *Nature* on a molecule they named teixobactin, found in a screen of uncultured bacteria, the roughly 99% of environmental species that standard methods won't grow. Teixobactin blocks cell wall synthesis by binding a highly conserved part of lipid II, the precursor of peptidoglycan, and lipid III, the precursor of cell wall teichoic acid. It grabs the building blocks, not a protein. In the experiments in that paper, the team did not obtain any mutants of *S. aureus* or *M. tuberculosis* resistant to it.

![Two cupped bare hands holding a heap of dark soil above more soil, in warm brown tones](/editorial/ideas/antibiotic-stopped-working-research-idea/2.jpg "Most environmental bacteria have never been grown in a laboratory. The teixobactin paper calls them an untapped source of new antibiotics.")

That result is worth reading precisely, because it's easy to inflate. "We did not obtain any mutants" describes one set of experiments, over a limited time, with particular bacteria and methods. It isn't proof that resistance can never appear. Teixobactin also isn't a medicine you can be prescribed: a search of ClinicalTrials.gov in November 2026 returned no registered studies for it. What the paper gives you is the reasoning, not a finished product. Aim at something the bacterium cannot easily redesign, and resistance gets harder to evolve.

## Docking molecules into PBP2a in four steps

You can't screen soil bacteria at home, and you shouldn't try to grow resistant bacteria at school. The computational side of the same field is genuinely open to you, and this version involves no human participants, so no ethics review is needed. (If you later add a survey about antibiotic use, you need your school's approval and consent from everyone you survey, with a parent's consent for anyone under 18. Many science fairs also require an institutional review board, or IRB, to approve the plan before you collect anything, so check your fair's rules first.)

**Step 1: pick one target and learn what it does.** PBP2a in MRSA is a good first choice because it's well studied. Give this a weekend of reading. You're finished when you can explain in one paragraph, without notes, what the protein does for the bacterium.

**Step 2: download its 3D shape.** Protein structures are free. The RCSB Protein Data Bank entry [1VQQ](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1VQQ) holds a soluble form of PBP2a from MRSA strain 27r, solved by X-ray crystallography at 1.80 Å (an ångström is a ten-billionth of a meter) by Lim and Strynadka and released in 2004. Open the coordinate file in [UCSF ChimeraX](https://www.cgl.ucsf.edu/chimerax/), free for academic, government, nonprofit and personal use. One detail matters: 1VQQ carries no drug, only cadmium and chloride ions, so it won't show you where a beta-lactam sits. Download [1MWT](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1MWT) as well, the same protein at 2.45 Å with penicillin G attached, and use it to locate the site. Allow an evening or two.

![A deep purple ribbon model of a protein with a small ball-and-stick molecule sitting in a pocket, against a blurred teal background](/editorial/ideas/antibiotic-stopped-working-research-idea/3.jpg "Docking asks whether a small molecule fits a pocket like this one. The protein in this render is not PBP2a; it stands in for the idea.")

**Step 3: dock molecules into that site.** [AutoDock Vina](https://vina.scripps.edu/) is an open-source docking program released under the Apache license. Docking means asking the software to try thousands of positions for a molecule inside a pocket and report the best-scoring fits. Vina won't read your downloaded files as they are: the protein and the molecule both have to be converted to its PDBQT format first, and the [Vina documentation](https://autodock-vina.readthedocs.io/en/latest/docking_basic.html) walks through that with the free Meeko scripts. Get your small molecules from [PubChem](https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), which is free and gives you an SDF file to start from (penicillin G is compound 5904). Center the search box on the site you found in 1MWT. Expect a weekend to install everything and get one clean run. After that, each molecule takes minutes on an ordinary laptop. Note the software versions you used, so your numbers can be reproduced.

**Step 4: compare scores with known antibiotics, carefully.** A docking score is a prediction, not a measurement, and two limits are worth stating plainly. First, beta-lactams don't simply sit in the pocket. They react with the active-site serine and stay chemically bonded to it, which is why the 1MWT structure is an acyl complex. Vina scores non-covalent fit, so it can't model that reaction. Second, the drug-free and penicillin-bound structures aren't identical, so which one you dock into is part of your method. Your score is a rough measure of shape and fit. Use it to compare molecules against each other under identical settings, and don't read it as how well a drug would work in a patient. Saying so makes your project stronger, not weaker. Budget one to two weeks for the comparison and the writing. The finished product is a short paper or a conference-style poster with a results table and two or three figures.

Two pointers for students in Korea. The same structure files are served from Japan by [PDBj](https://pdbj.org/mine/summary/1vqq). For Korean resistance figures rather than American ones, start with Kor-GLASS, the national surveillance system built to match the WHO one. Its first-year report in *Eurosurveillance* counted 1.6 bloodstream infections per 10,000 patient-days from methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* in inpatients, May 2016 to April 2017.

## How narrow an antibiotic question should be

The gap between an interesting topic and a project you can finish is usually the width of your question.

| Too big | Workable |
| --- | --- |
| Can I design an antibiotic bacteria cannot resist? | How do AutoDock Vina scores against PBP2a rank ten published beta-lactams whose activity against MRSA is already reported? |
| Why does MRSA resist antibiotics? | Does the same molecule score differently against the drug-free structure (1VQQ) and the penicillin-bound structure (1MWT), and by how much? |
| Find a better drug than penicillin | Do molecules reported in the literature as PBP2a binders score better than a control set of similar-sized molecules with no reported activity? |

You can answer each question on the right with free software and a laptop, and each gives you a table somebody else could reproduce. That's what a good docking project delivers: not a cure, but a result with its limits written down.

A strong paper on resistance doesn't have to start with docking, or with new data at all. A literature review works from studies other labs have already published. You could ask how follow-up studies of teixobactin and its synthetic analogues tested for resistance: which bacteria, how many days of repeated exposure, and whether anyone found resistant mutants. Find the papers on [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) and [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/), then compare their methods sections. A research proposal designs the lab work a school can't safely host. Your docking scores leave the next question open: does a top-scoring molecule actually stop MRSA from growing? A proposal states that question, describes the method (finding the lowest concentration that stops growth, in MRSA and in a methicillin-susceptible strain), lists the compounds and bacterial strains you'd need, and names the biosafety approval a university lab requires before handling MRSA.

Your infection was the question. Now research it.

Students who want to work on this kind of chemistry with a faculty mentor can look at [Quantitative Analysis of Biochemistry](/research/program/cmttsjkvy0000eoptn4ppvad1), taught by Jason Sello, Professor of Pharmaceutical Chemistry at the University of California San Francisco (UCSF). title: Is my bus really late every morning? How to research it with a phone log
excerpt: Turn "my bus is always late" into a data project: log arrivals for a month, check open bus data, and test whether mornings are really worse.
content:
"I'm sure my bus is late every single morning." You hear it at bus stops everywhere, and it usually stays a complaint. But it's also a claim about the world, and claims can be checked. How would you test it with data? Here's how to turn that morning frustration into a small research project you can finish in about six weeks with a phone, a free spreadsheet and public transit data.

## Why five minutes at a bus stop can feel like twenty

Time stretches when nothing happens, and researchers have measured it. In a study published in 2011, Kari Watkins and colleagues watched riders arrive at bus stops in the Seattle area, recorded how long each person actually waited, and then asked how long they thought they'd waited. Riders without real-time arrival information said they had waited longer than measured. Riders who used live arrival information on their phones didn't overestimate.

So a feeling is weak evidence. "Late" has to become a number before you can test it, and that raises a real research question. Late compared with what?

There are two common answers:

- **Compared with the timetable.** The schedule says 7:42 and the bus comes at 7:49, so it's 7 minutes late.
- **Compared with the planned gap between buses.** If a bus should come every 8 minutes, riders care whether the next one really comes within about 8 minutes. When two buses arrive together and then nothing comes for 20 minutes, the timetable tells you little about how long people waited.

Picking a definition is a researcher's first decision, and different choices can give different answers about the same bus.

## Write it down every morning, before you trust your memory

Write the time down at the stop, every morning, right away. Not later from memory, because your memory of the month is exactly what you're testing.

Researchers call this an operational definition: before collecting anything, you decide what you'll measure and how. What counts as "arrived" (the doors open at your stop)? Which clock (always your phone)? What counts as late (say, more than 3 minutes after the scheduled time)? Fix the rules first. Once you see the data, it's tempting to pick whichever definition agrees with what you already believed.

Also note the time you reach the stop. That separates two things: how late the bus was, and how long you waited. A bus can be on time while you wait 12 minutes because you came early.

![A hand holds a white smartphone showing a stopwatch app at 00:00.00 with a green Start button, in front of a blurred green plant](/editorial/ideas/bus-late-every-morning-research-idea/1.jpg "The tool for the first step is already in your pocket: the same phone clock, used the same way every morning.")

## New York already counts the gaps between its buses

Transit agencies track buses too, and New York publishes the results. The New York State open data portal hosts the MTA Bus Wait Assessment dataset, covering New York City bus routes from January 2015 to October 2026. Each row is one route in one month, split by weekday or weekend and by peak or off-peak hours, with the route's borough, the number of trips scheduled and the number that passed.

The MTA describes Wait Assessment as a measure of "how evenly buses are spaced." Its overview document for the dataset sets the standard: a gap between two buses passes if it's no more than 3 minutes longer than the scheduled gap in the morning (7 to 9 a.m.) and afternoon (4 to 7 p.m.) peaks, and no more than 5 minutes longer at other times. The numbers come from the MTA's Bus Time tracking data.

Adding up the dataset's own columns for 2025 gives 48,760,250 passing trips out of 69,458,058 scheduled. That's 70.2%, or about 7 in 10 gaps between New York City buses meeting the MTA standard.

The MTA lists the limits itself: the measure isn't weighted by how many people wait at each stop, doesn't separate a small gap from a major delay, and isn't a true measurement of how long riders wait.

![An MTA express bus with an orange SIM3c destination sign drives toward the camera on a New York City street at dusk, with a bus stop sign on the left](/editorial/ideas/bus-late-every-morning-research-idea/2.jpg "New York's open data reports, route by route and month by month, how many gaps between buses met the MTA standard.")

## A six-week plan that starts at your own bus stop

### Step 1: Log arrivals for one month (4 to 5 weeks, 2 minutes a day)

Make a [Google Sheet](https://workspace.google.com/products/sheets/) with one row per trip: date, weekday, morning or afternoon, scheduled time (if there's a timetable), when you reached the stop, when the bus came, and notes such as rain or an exam day. Log the ride home too. Twenty school days give you about 20 mornings to compare with 20 afternoons.

Only you and a public bus are involved, so no one else's consent is needed. If you later ask classmates or other riders how long they think they waited, that's research with people. It needs your school's approval, an IRB (ethics board) review where required, and consent from each person, including a parent's consent for anyone under 18. Don't film or photograph other riders.

### Step 2: Get your city's open bus data (one or two evenings)

- **New York City:** open the [MTA Bus Wait Assessment dataset](https://data.ny.gov/d/v4z4-2h6n), filter it to your route and export a CSV file. It shows how often your route's gaps passed each month. It has no arrival times. The overview warns that pre-2019 numbers used an older method, so don't compare them directly with later years.
- **Live arrival times:** [MTA Bus Time](https://bustime.mta.info/) shows where New York buses are right now, and its free [developer API](https://bustime.mta.info/developers) sends the same data to a program once you request a key. Many agencies share live data in a format called [GTFS Realtime](https://gtfs.org/documentation/realtime/reference/), which includes vehicle positions and predicted arrivals.
- **Korea:** Seoul publishes real-time bus arrival predictions through its Bus Arrival search service on the national [Public Data Portal](https://www.data.go.kr/data/15000314/openapi.do) (in Korean). It's free with a service key.

### Step 3: Compare the schedule with real times (one weekend)

For each trip, subtract the scheduled time from the real arrival time. That's minutes late; a negative number means early. In Google Sheets, =(F2-D2)*1440 turns the gap between two times into minutes (format that column as Number). If your route only promises "every 10 minutes," use your own wait instead.

One log has a limit: you see one bus per trip. Measuring gaps the way the MTA does needs several buses in a row, so you'd have to watch the stop longer or save a live feed with a short script. That's an extension, not a requirement.

![An LED board under a station roof at dusk shows two trains to Hacıosman due in 1 and 8 minutes, with a red scrolling message below](/editorial/ideas/bus-late-every-morning-research-idea/3.jpg "A countdown board turns waiting into minutes. Your log does the same, one trip at a time.")

### Step 4: Test whether mornings are really worse (a few hours)

Put mornings and afternoons side by side, one row per school day, skipping days where one is missing. Plot one dot per trip. Compare the medians (the middle values) first, since one terrible day can't drag a median around. Then try Google Sheets' [T.TEST](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6055837) function. With mornings in column B and afternoons in column C, =T.TEST(B2:B21, C2:C21, 2, 1) runs a two-tailed, paired test: it matches each morning with the afternoon of the same day. T.TEST compares the averages (means) and gives a p-value: the chance of seeing a difference at least this large if mornings and afternoons were really the same. A p-value below 0.05 is usually called statistically significant. With 20 days and a few very late buses, treat it as a first hint, not proof.

Watch for unfair comparisons. In the 2025 New York data, about 65% of trips in the peak rows passed Wait Assessment, against about 72% off-peak. Rush hours look worse. But the overview gives peak hours a stricter test (3 minutes, not 5), so part of that gap may come from the ruler rather than the buses. The dataset's short column notes mention only the 3-minute rule, so read the full documentation before you compare. In your project, use one definition of late for mornings and afternoons.

The result is a one-page poster or a short paper of 4 to 6 pages: one chart, one table, a clear definition of "late" and an honest paragraph on limits, such as data from one route and one rider.

## Making "always late" something you can test

Narrow it to one route, one time window, one definition and an amount of data you can actually collect.

| Too big | Workable |
| --- | --- |
| Are buses in my city unreliable? | Over four weeks of school days, does my morning bus arrive more than 3 minutes after its scheduled time more often than my afternoon bus? |
| Why does waiting feel so long? | I start a stopwatch at the stop, guess my wait without looking, then check. Over 20 trips, are my guesses too long? |
| Which city has the best buses? | In New York's 2025 data, using only weekday off-peak rows, do routes in one borough pass Wait Assessment more often than another borough's? |

The third question needs no bus ride, so it works for a student anywhere. One caution from the dataset's overview: Queens routes were redesigned in summer 2025, so compare them across that year with care.

The questions in the table all call for new numbers, which makes them original research. A literature review and a research proposal fit bus delays just as well.

In a **literature review**, you compare published studies to answer one question. Have studies outside Seattle also found that live arrival information stops riders overestimating their waits? Note how each measured the real wait, since a guess means little without a timed one. On [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/), try "real-time information" together with "perceived wait time".

A **research proposal** plans a study too big to run from one stop. Do countdown screens change how long riders think they waited? You could propose that an agency add screens at a random half of the stops on several routes for a school year, while observers time riders' real waits and a short survey asks how long each wait felt. List the data (timed waits and survey answers from stops with and without screens) and the approval: an IRB review and each rider's consent, plus a parent's for anyone under 18.

## Your stop, your data

Your bus was the question. Now research it.

At CRI, students research with professors in many fields, such as biology, economics, chemistry and history, and the question and the paper are their own. That paper can be original research, a literature review or a research proposal. For the details, see [CRI's research programs](/research).

## Sources

- Metropolitan Transportation Authority (2026). MTA Bus Wait Assessment Overview, version 1.1.2 [dataset documentation]. New York State Open Data. [link](https://data.ny.gov/api/views/v4z4-2h6n/files/d019faed-a8ed-4849-aef9-bb464db6864a?download=true&filename=MTA_BusWaitAssessment_Overview.pdf)
- Metropolitan Transportation Authority. MTA Bus Wait Assessment Data Dictionary [dataset documentation]. New York State Open Data. [link](https://data.ny.gov/api/views/v4z4-2h6n/files/19af37ee-1646-49d0-9957-520515915dc3?download=true&filename=MTA_BusWaitAssessment_DataDictionary.pdf)
- Watkins, K. E., Ferris, B., Borning, A., Rutherford, G. S., & Layton, D. (2011). Where Is My Bus? Impact of mobile real-time information on the perceived and actual wait time of transit riders. *Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice*, 45(8), 839-848. [link](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tra.2011.06.010)
- Metropolitan Transportation Authority. MTA Bus Time. [link](https://bustime.mta.info/)
- Metropolitan Transportation Authority. MTA Bus Time developer API. [link](https://bustime.mta.info/developers)
- GTFS. GTFS Realtime reference. gtfs.org. [link](https://gtfs.org/documentation/realtime/reference/)

- Google. T.TEST function. Google Docs Editors Help. [link](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6055837)

title: Does quizzing yourself beat rereading? Memory research you can run at school
excerpt: Rereading feels like studying, but in a 2006 study recall tests worked better a week later. Two word lists and a group of classmates are enough to test it.
content:
"I study all night and still forget everything." It comes up in the week before every exam, often with a worse thought attached: maybe my memory is just bad. A psychologist would check something else first: the way you study may matter more than the hours, and you can test that yourself.

Below is one well-known study, and a plan you could carry out with classmates.

## Why rereading feels like learning

You read the chapter. Then you read it again, maybe five times. Each pass feels easier. On Friday, in front of a blank answer sheet, much of it has faded.

Two skills are at work. Recognizing means seeing something and knowing you've seen it before. Recalling means producing it from memory with nothing in front of you. Rereading gives you a lot of practice at the first and little at the second, but an essay or short-answer question asks for the second. Feeling familiar is not the same as remembering.

That's a testable claim: the method that feels best in the moment may not be the one that lasts. In the study below, students who spent every study period rereading were the most confident they'd remember the passage a week later, and they remembered the least.

![A study desk at night lit by a glowing lamp and a candle, with a vase of flowers, a cup of pens, a small clock and a cup of tea](/editorial/ideas/quizzing-vs-rereading-memory-research/1.jpg "A late night at the desk can feel productive, but how familiar your notes feel can be a poor guide to what you'll recall a week later.")

## Two study methods, one change, a test later

Memory researchers test "what makes memory stick?" with a controlled experiment: two study methods, only one change between them, and a test later.

- **The one change** is the study method, called the independent variable. Some material is reread. Other material is practiced with a recall test, where you write down everything you remember on a blank page.
- **Everything else stays the same**, including the time spent and the final test.
- **The outcome** is how much people recall on that final test, called the dependent variable.

"Later" matters. Five minutes after studying, rereading can look better because the material is still fresh. What you care about is what's left days later.

A good design also rules out easy explanations. Taking a quiz is one more pass through the material, so maybe testing helps only because of that extra look. To check, Roediger and Karpicke gave their rereaders the full passage again each time the other students took a test. Test-takers saw only what they could pull from memory, with no feedback. If anything, that favored rereading.

## The 2006 experiment where rereading won, then lost

Henry L. Roediger III and Jeffrey D. Karpicke of Washington University in St. Louis published "[Test-Enhanced Learning](https://psychology.ecu.edu/wp-content/pv-uploads/sites/216/2019/03/Roediger-Karpicke-2006.pdf)" in *Psychological Science* in March 2006. In their second experiment, 180 undergraduates aged 18 to 24 learned one short science passage ("The Sun" or "Sea Otters," from a TOEFL preparation book). Over four back-to-back periods, each student either spent all four reading the passage, read it for three and then took one recall test, or read it for one and then took three recall tests. Reading periods lasted 5 minutes. Half took the final test 5 minutes later and half came back after a week, making six groups of 30.

After 5 minutes, rereading won: 83% of the passage's ideas recalled, against 71% for the read-once, test-three-times group. After one week the order flipped. The repeated-testing group recalled 61% and the repeated-reading group 40%, even though rereaders had read through the passage 14.2 times on average and the tested group only 3.4 times.

Confidence went the other way. On a 7-point scale, rereaders rated how well they'd remember the passage in a week at 4.8, against 4.0 for the repeated-testing group.

The limits are real. These were students at one American university, tested in small groups on two short passages, with 30 people per group. The final test was the same kind of recall test the tested group had practiced, which the authors see as part of why testing helped. The study can't tell you how big the effect would be for a semester of high school chemistry or for younger students.

![A small ring-bound pack of blank white flashcards on a plain white surface](/editorial/ideas/quizzing-vs-rereading-memory-research/2.jpg "A recall test can be as simple as a blank card or sheet: the work is in pulling the words out of memory, not in looking at them again.")

## A word-list experiment for your classmates

Your version differs from the 61% versus 40% result in two ways: word lists instead of prose, and one quiz instead of three. The closer match is the paper's first experiment, where each student used both methods, one per passage, and a single recall test gave 56% recall after a week against 42% for rereading. Most earlier testing-effect studies used word lists, the authors note, but don't expect your numbers to match theirs. Your result is what you'll report.

**Step 1: Make two lists of 20 words (about 2 hours).** If one list is easier, you'll be measuring the lists, not the methods. Use common, concrete nouns of similar length that aren't related to each other. For Korean-speaking classmates, the National Institute of Korean Language's free [vocabulary list for learners of Korean](https://www.korean.go.kr/front_eng/down/down_02V.do?etc_seq=70) (2003, in Korean) has 5,965 words with a frequency rank, a part of speech and a level from A to C, so you can take all 40 nouns from one level. For English, Ghent University's [SUBTLEX-US](https://www.ugent.be/pp/experimentele-psychologie/en/research/documents/subtlexus) gives frequencies counted from about 51 million words of film and TV subtitles. After approval (Step 3), a short pilot with two or three volunteers can show whether one list is clearly easier.

**Step 2: Reread one list, quiz the other (about 25 minutes per session).** Your classmates study List A for 2 minutes, then reread it for 2 minutes. They study List B for 2 minutes, then spend 2 minutes writing every word they remember on a blank sheet, with no answers shown afterward. Between periods, give 2 minutes of simple math (the original study used multiplication problems) so people can't silently repeat the words. Make four versions of the session so that each list is the quizzed one for half your classmates, and the quizzed list comes first for half. That's counterbalancing, and it keeps an easier list or the order from deciding your result.

**Step 3: Test classmates, with school approval (2 to 4 weeks to arrange).** Get approval before you run any session, including the pilot. Ask your teacher and school, have your plan reviewed by an IRB (an ethics review board) where required, and collect written consent, including a parent's consent for anyone under 18. Let anyone stop at any time, and record scores under code numbers, not names. Aim for 20 or more classmates; with fewer, you can easily miss a real difference because of chance variation. Ask everyone not to practice the words during the week.

**Step 4: Compare scores one week later (15 minutes of testing, then an afternoon of analysis).** Ask each classmate to write every word they remember from both lists on one blank sheet. When you score, sort the words by list and give one point per correct word. In Google Sheets, put one classmate per row, one column per list, and use AVERAGE on each column. `=T.TEST(B2:B25, C2:C25, 2, 1)` runs a [paired t-test](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6055837?hl=en): 2 means two-tailed, and 1 means paired, because the same people produced both scores. You get a p-value, roughly the chance of seeing a difference at least this large if both methods worked equally well. [JASP](https://jasp-stats.org/), free software supported by the University of Amsterdam, runs the same test under T-Tests.

You'll end up with a bar chart of two averages, a p-value, and notes on what might have affected the result. That's enough for a research poster or a short paper of four to six pages. A small or reversed difference still counts. Explaining it is part of the work.

![A printed sheet of sample line, bar and pie charts on a dark desk, between a laptop and a row of colored pencils](/editorial/ideas/quizzing-vs-rereading-memory-research/3.jpg "Your main result can be one chart: the average score for the reread list next to the average for the quizzed list.")

## What to ask instead of "how should I study?"

Spell out the people, the two conditions, what you'll measure, and when.

| Too big | Workable |
| --- | --- |
| What is the best way to study? | Do 10th graders recall more words from a list they were quizzed on than from a list they reread, one week later? |
| Does testing help memory? | With word lists, does rereading win on a test 5 minutes later while quizzing wins after a week, as Roediger and Karpicke found with prose? |
| Why do students trust rereading? | Right after studying, do classmates predict higher scores for the reread list, and how close are those guesses to their scores a week later? |

For the second question, you'll need an extra group who take the final test after 5 minutes. For the third, you'll add one question at the end of your session: "How many words from each list will you remember next week?"

The testing effect suits a literature review or a research proposal as well as it suits an experiment.

A **literature review** answers a question from published studies. Did quizzing help as much in middle and high school classrooms, and did those studies measure it with free recall, multiple choice or unit exams? Search [ERIC](https://eric.ed.gov/), the US Department of Education's education research library, or [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/) for "retrieval practice," researchers' term for studying by recalling.

A **research proposal** plans a semester-long classroom study. Would high school chemistry classes that open each lesson with a short ungraded quiz score higher on the semester final than classes that reread? Your proposal would pose that question and lay out the method (classes at several schools assigned at random to quizzing or rereading), the data (final exam scores and earlier grades), and what has to be approved first: an IRB review, school permission, and consent from students and parents.

Your forgetting was the question. Now research it.

CRI students research with professors in many fields, such as biology, economics, chemistry and history, and write their own paper, from original research to literature reviews and research proposals. If a question like this one keeps coming back to you, [CRI's research programs](/research) show how students turn it into a finished project.

## Sources

[link](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x) (free copy: [PDF](https://psychology.ecu.edu/wp-content/pv-uploads/sites/216/2019/03/Roediger-Karpicke-2006.pdf))

title: Why do knees tear? An ACL study high school students can film
excerpt: In a study of men's pro soccer, 88% of filmed ACL tears had no direct hit to the knee. A phone, a box and free software can measure knee angles on landing.
content:
"I tore my ACL playing soccer." It tends to come with a surgery date and months on the bench. Often nobody even touched the knee. The player planted a foot, turned or landed, and the knee gave way. How do engineers and sports scientists work out why a knee tears, and could you start studying it with your phone?

## What happens inside the knee when an ACL tears

The ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) is a band of tissue that runs diagonally through the middle of your knee. It keeps your shinbone (tibia) from sliding out in front of your thighbone (femur). The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that most ACL injuries happen without a direct hit to the knee, most often while pivoting, cutting (changing direction suddenly) or landing from a jump.

Not every tear needs an operation. If the knee stays stable and the patient avoids pivoting and cutting sports, physical therapy alone can be a reasonable choice. Surgery usually replaces the torn ligament with a piece of tendon, and recovery is slow: most patients are allowed back to full sports within 6 to 12 months.

![Black-and-white close-up of a leg in a hinged knee brace with a lattice shell, resting on a couch beside a patterned cushion](/editorial/ideas/acl-knee-landing-research-idea/1.jpg "Recovery from ACL reconstruction is slow: most patients return to full sports within 6 to 12 months.")

Slow-motion video of these injuries often shows the same shape. The knee caves inward. Seen from the front, it drops toward the middle of the body while the foot stays planted further out. Researchers call this knee valgus. Seeing it at the moment of injury doesn't prove it caused the tear, but it tells researchers where to look first.

## Film the move, measure the angle

Biomechanics is the study of forces and movement in living bodies. Knee researchers often either study real injuries on video, frame by frame, or bring athletes into a lab and film a safe, repeatable move, usually a box landing, with skin markers and several cameras that build a 3D model of the leg.

A 2005 lab study by Hewett and colleagues measured 205 female soccer, basketball and volleyball players landing from a jump. The nine who later tore an ACL had landed with a knee abduction angle (the lab's 3D measure of the inward collapse) 8 degrees greater than the 196 who didn't.

Nine injuries isn't a big sample, though. A much larger Norwegian study (Krosshaug and colleagues, 2016) tested 782 elite female soccer and handball players with a similar drop-jump test and recorded 42 new non-contact ACL injuries among the 710 it analyzed. The test couldn't predict who would get hurt.

## 134 filmed ACL tears in Italian professional soccer

The study behind our carousel is Della Villa and colleagues (2020), published in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine*. The team found 148 ACL injuries across 10 seasons of professional men's football (soccer) in Italy and analyzed video of 134 of them. Three reviewers judged each video independently:

- 59 injuries (44%) were non-contact, meaning nobody touched the player.
- 59 (44%) were indirect contact: the player was bumped somewhere else, mostly on the upper body, just before the injury.
- 16 (12%) were direct contact to the knee.

That's 88% without a direct hit to the knee. In the injuries the team could analyze movement by movement, knee valgus loading was the dominant pattern (83 cases, 81%). Pressing and tackling an opponent was the most common situation (55 cases); landing from a jump was the least common of the four main ones (8 cases).

![A worn neon-yellow and gray soccer ball on dark artificial turf at night, with a fence, a floodlight and small distant figures behind it](/editorial/ideas/acl-knee-landing-research-idea/2.jpg "In the 2020 Italian study, 88% of the 134 filmed ACL injuries happened without a direct hit to the knee.")

Still, video shows only what happened just before an injury, not why one player tore an ACL while another in the same situation didn't. And it covers professional men only. Teenagers and women's soccer may look different.

## How to measure knee angles with a phone and free software

You can't safely recreate a professional tackle in a school gym. A landing, with supervision, is different. Landings were a small share of the Italian injuries, but they're a standard lab task because they're easy to repeat. Your measure is the frontal plane projection angle (FPPA): seen from the front, the angle between a hip-to-knee line and a knee-to-ankle line. A straight leg reads close to 0 degrees, and the number grows as the knee drops inward. It's a simple 2D stand-in for the lab's 3D measures, and it reflects the sideways load on the knee only roughly (Straub and Powers, 2022).

**Step 1: Pick one move (about a week).** Use the drop vertical jump: stand on a box about 30 cm high, drop off, land on both feet and jump straight up. A 2019 study of adolescent male athletes used this task as a screening test, filmed it from the front and analyzed it in Kinovea (Mohd Azhar and colleagues). Read it, plus the Herrington and Munro abstracts in our Sources. Then write a one-page plan: the task, the box height, the number of jumps, where your camera goes and which frame you'll measure. Practice on your own landings first.

**Step 2: Film classmates, with school approval (2 to 4 weeks for approval, one or two short sessions to film).** You'll need your school's approval and written consent from each volunteer, plus a parent's or guardian's consent for anyone who is a minor. Some schools and science fairs also need an IRB review before you collect any data: an institutional review board checks that research with people is safe and fair. Ask a PE teacher to supervise. Leave out anyone with knee pain or a past knee injury, and frame the shot from just above the hips down so no faces are recorded. Keep the videos private, and delete them when you're done. Set your phone on a tripod at knee height, a few meters away, facing the landing spot straight on, and use slow motion if your phone has it. A test of Kinovea on a wire model of a leg recommends that straight-on view (Puig-Diví and colleagues, 2019). Small stickers on the front of the hip bone, the center of the knee and the middle of the ankle mark your points. Ten to twenty volunteers doing three jumps each, with a minute of rest between jumps, is a workable first study.

![A smartphone on a tall tripod standing on a yellow circle of an empty sports court, next to a black bag](/editorial/ideas/acl-knee-landing-research-idea/3.jpg "A phone and a tripod are all the camera gear you need. For landings, lower the phone to knee height and point it straight at the landing spot.")

**Step 3: Measure knee angles in Kinovea (two or three evenings).** [Kinovea](https://www.kinovea.org/) is free, open-source sport-analysis software that measures angles, distances and times. Use one frame rule for every clip, such as the lowest point of the landing, when the knee is most bent. Place the angle tool on the three stickers. Kinovea gives you the angle at the knee; subtract it from 180 to get the FPPA, and record it as negative if the knee sits outside the hip-to-ankle line. Measure every clip twice, a few days apart, without looking at your first numbers. Munro and colleagues found that one person's FPPA had to change by more than about 7.5 to 9 degrees to count as real, not measurement error. Kinovea needs Windows and won't work on Macs with Apple chips. On a Mac, use the free [Tracker](https://opensourcephysics.github.io/tracker-website/) from Open Source Physics, which has a protractor tool. On a Chromebook, try [Tracker Online](https://opensourcephysics.github.io/tracker-online/) in your browser.

**Step 4: Compare with published landing data (one to two weeks).** Herrington and Munro (2010) measured 100 physically active adults aged 18 to 28 and suggested that a typical drop-jump FPPA falls between 7 and 13 degrees for women and between 3 and 8 degrees for men. Put your group averages next to those ranges and say why a gap might appear: their participants were adults, and their setup may differ from yours. Don't tell any classmate their number means they're "at risk." The Norwegian study showed this kind of test can't predict that. For Korean studies, search [RISS](https://www.riss.kr/), the Korea Education and Research Information Service's database (in Korean), using the Korean words for "landing" and "knee valgus." You'll come away with a table of angles, a chart with each person as a dot, and a 6 to 8 page paper or a poster.

## Turning a sore knee into a research question

Professional research teams are still working out why ACLs tear. A good first filming project asks something you can answer with one box, one phone and a few weeks.

| Too big | Workable |
| --- | --- |
| Why do ACLs tear? | Do classmates show a different drop-jump FPPA on their dominant and non-dominant legs? |
| Are girls more likely to tear an ACL? | Do girls and boys in our school's sports clubs differ in drop-jump FPPA? |
| Does being tired cause knee injuries? | Does drop-jump FPPA change in the same students after two minutes of jump rope? |

Every question on the right fixes the move, the measure and the people. That's what makes it answerable in one school term.

The two screening studies above can also start a literature review or a research proposal.

A **literature review** compares published studies, and these two already disagree. Hewett's team linked a bigger inward collapse to later tears; Krosshaug's found a similar test couldn't predict them. Did later screening studies agree with either, and did that depend on who was tested (teenage girls, adult women or men) or on 3D versus 2D measurement? Useful search terms on [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) and [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/) are "drop vertical jump" and "ACL injury."

A **research proposal** plans a study over several seasons. Does phone-measured FPPA predict ACL tears in high school girls? Krosshaug's 710 players had only 42 non-contact tears, so you'd film a whole regional soccer league before the season and record doctor-confirmed tears for three seasons. Name the data (angles, hours played, injury reports) and the approvals: an IRB review, each player's agreement and a parent's consent.

Your knee was the question. Now research it.

Students at CRI work with professors in many fields, such as biology, economics, chemistry and history, and finish with a paper they write themselves on a question of their own. It might be a research proposal, a literature review or original research. Read how that works in [CRI's research programs](/research).

title: Are you a different person in Korean and English? A bilingual research project
excerpt: Feel more outgoing in English than in Korean? Psychologists call it cultural frame switching, and one free personality test in both languages can measure it.
content:
"I feel like a different person in Korean and in English." It's a common feeling among students who switch between the two languages every day. In one language you might joke more and speak up faster. In the other you might pick your words with more care. Which language does which is different for each person.

Does the language you speak change how you think? Psychologists have measured one part of it, and their method is simple enough to copy with free tools.

## Louder in English, softer in Korean? What psychologists call it

Psychologists often describe personality with five broad traits, the Big Five:

- **Extraversion:** how outgoing and talkative you are.
- **Agreeableness:** how warm and cooperative you are.
- **Conscientiousness:** how organized and careful you are.
- **Emotional stability:** how calm you stay. Its opposite is called neuroticism.
- **Intellect or imagination,** often called openness: how curious you are about ideas.

You rate short statements for how well they describe you, such as "Start conversations" or "Feel comfortable around people." So "louder in English" turns into a question you can test: does the same person score higher on extraversion when the test is in English?

The idea has a name: **cultural frame switching**. If you've taken in two cultures, as many bilinguals have, cues around you can shift the way you interpret the world, and a language is one of those cues.

First, a limit. The studies below don't measure how you *think*. They measure how you describe yourself on a questionnaire in each language. That's narrower, but you can count it.

![A single light switch on a textured orange wall, lit from the side so that it casts a sharp shadow](/editorial/ideas/bilingual-personality-korean-english-research/1.jpg "The switch is only a metaphor: in the 2006 study, scores shifted between languages, but an outgoing person did not turn into a shy one.")

## Same person, two languages: how researchers compare

The core method is a within-subject design: every participant takes the same test in both languages, and you compare each person with themselves. If one group took it in Korean and another in English, a gap could just mean the English group had more outgoing people in it. Same-person comparison removes that problem.

You'll need to control two more things. **Both versions must mean the same thing,** or the score can move because of the wording, not the person. Researchers check this with back-translation: a second translator turns the Korean version back into English without seeing the original, and the two English versions are compared. **The order must be balanced.** If everyone takes the English test second, you can't tell a language effect from the effect of doing the same test twice. So half the group starts in Korean and half in English, which is called counterbalancing.

## The 2006 study with Spanish–English bilinguals

A well-known test of this idea is "Do bilinguals have two personalities?", a 2006 paper in the *Journal of Research in Personality* by Ramírez-Esparza, Gosling, Benet-Martínez, Potter and Pennebaker.

The first of its four studies compared monolingual speakers in the US and Mexico. The other three tested separate groups of Spanish–English bilinguals living in the US and Mexico. Each bilingual filled in a Big Five questionnaire twice, once in English and once in Spanish.

In English, the bilinguals scored higher on extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness, and slightly lower on neuroticism. The pattern held in all three bilingual groups. It also matched the monolingual results, where English speakers scored higher on those first three traits. According to the BPS Research Digest summary, the researchers checked that the translation itself wasn't causing the effect. The public summaries don't say how big the shifts were, so read the full paper before quoting numbers.

There are limits, though. Scores shifted, but the same summary reports that the overall shape of people's personalities did not change much: someone outgoing in Spanish was still among the more outgoing in English. With only one language pair, the study can't tell us whether Korean–English bilinguals shift too, or in which direction. A later study by Chen and Bond (2010), with Chinese–English bilinguals in Hong Kong, found that language mattered, and so did the ethnicity of the person they were talking with. Its authors call the question controversial, so treat it as something to test, not a settled fact.

![A white sheet with three square boxes, the top one ticked with a red check mark, on a pale blue background](/editorial/ideas/bilingual-personality-korean-english-research/2.jpg "A Big Five test is a list of short statements you rate, and the comparison comes from giving the same list twice, once in each language.")

## Running the test with free IPIP forms

Plan on about two months part-time, mostly waiting for approval and answers.

### 1. Use the free IPIP personality test (one to two hours)

The International Personality Item Pool (IPIP) is a public-domain set of personality items. Its [home page](https://ipip.ori.org/) says you can copy, edit, translate or use them for any purpose without permission or fees. Use the [IPIP Big-Five factor markers](https://ipip.ori.org/newBigFive5broadKey.htm): the 50-item version has 10 items per trait. The site shows a [sample 50-item questionnaire](https://ipip.ori.org/new_ipip-50-item-scale.htm) and [how to score it](https://ipip.ori.org/newScoringInstructions.htm): each answer gets 1 to 5 points, from "Very Inaccurate" to "Very Accurate," reversed for items that point the other way, such as "Don't talk a lot," and the points add up to a score for each trait.

### 2. Get Korean and English versions (an afternoon)

You don't have to translate anything. The IPIP [translations page](https://ipip.ori.org/newTranslations.htm) lists a Korean back-translation of the 100 Big-Five factor marker items by Dr. In-Sue Oh, with help from Kibeom Lee and Jong-Goo Lee. The [Korean items](https://ipip.ori.org/KoreanBig-FiveFactorMarkers.htm) sit next to the English ones, so you can pick the Korean wording of your 50 items. That page notes that the 50-item version was used in a 2013 study of job performance in South Korea.

But the IPIP project says no one connected to it has checked the accuracy of its translations, so read every pair yourself. For example, the Korean wording of "Am the life of the party" is closer to "I enjoy going to all kinds of gatherings." Note pairs like this; you'll need them later.

Then build two online forms, for example in [Google Forms](https://www.google.com/forms/about/), with the same items, order and five answer choices: one fully in Korean, instructions included, and one fully in English.

### 3. Survey bilinguals, with school approval (two to four weeks)

This step involves people, so talk to a teacher before you collect anything. You'll need school approval, an IRB review where your school or country requires one (an IRB is a committee that checks that research with people is safe and fair), consent from every participant, and parental consent for anyone under 18.

Look for students who use both languages comfortably, such as those at an international school. Ask a few background questions: years lived in an English-speaking country, the language spoken at home, which language feels stronger. Don't collect names or emails; have each student make up a code for both forms so you can match them. With ten people you'll struggle to tell a small difference from chance, so recruit as many as you can.

### 4. Swap language order, compare scores (one to two weeks)

Split your participants into two groups at random. Group A takes the Korean form first, Group B the English form. Leave about a week between sessions so people are less likely to repeat answers from memory.

Score the five traits in each language. Then load the data into [JASP](https://jasp-stats.org/), a free, open-source statistics program, and run a paired samples t-test for each trait: it asks whether the average Korean–English gap within the same people is bigger than chance would explain. JASP's repeated measures ANOVA lets you add the order group as a second factor, to check that the result doesn't depend on which test came first. With five tests, one could look different by chance alone, so say that in your limits.

You end up with a table of trait averages in each language, one chart, and a four- to six-page paper or a poster. No difference is a result too, and it's worth reporting.

![A teenager seen from behind in a striped shirt, working on a laptop at a white desk with a white lamp, against a pale blue-green wall](/editorial/ideas/bilingual-personality-korean-english-research/3.jpg "Once the surveys are in, the rest of the project is desk work: scoring two forms and comparing them in a free statistics program.")

## Measuring "a different person"

"Does language change who I am?" can't be answered in one study. To test it with a survey, you'll need a group, a measure and a comparison.

| Too big | Workable |
| --- | --- |
| Does the language you speak change how you think? | Do Korean–English bilingual students score higher on IPIP extraversion in English than in Korean, with test order balanced? |
| Does living abroad change your personality? | Is the gap between English and Korean extraversion scores larger for students who have lived longer in an English-speaking country? |
| Are personality tests fair across languages? | Which of the 50 IPIP items show the biggest Korean–English gap, and do those items differ in meaning between the two versions? |

All three use the same two forms, and the third uses your translation notes: if the biggest gaps sit on items whose meaning shifted, part of the "different person" result may come from the test, not from you.

Since no single study settles the question, reading and comparing the published ones is a paper in itself: a **literature review**. Does the shift the 2006 study reported for Spanish–English bilinguals show up in other language pairs, such as Chinese–English or Korean–English? Did any of the studies check behavior as well as questionnaire answers? Search [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/) and [APA PsycInfo](https://www.apa.org/pubs/databases/psycinfo), the American Psychological Association's database (usually through a library), for "cultural frame switching" and "bilingual personality."

A **research proposal** designs a study that would take years to run. Does the Korean–English extraversion gap grow within the same students as they spend more years abroad? A survey you run once can't show that. The plan could follow Korean students who move to English-speaking schools, giving both IPIP forms every year for three years with the order balanced. The proposal would list the data (yearly scores and time abroad for a few hundred students at several schools) and what it needs before anyone is enrolled: an IRB review, permission from each school and parental consent for anyone under 18.

## Start with your own two languages

Your bilingual self was the question. Now research it.

At CRI, a student works with a professor in one of many fields, such as biology, economics, chemistry and history, and writes their own paper, with original research, a literature review and a research proposal all open to them. For how the programs are organized, see [CRI's research programs](/research).

## Sources

- International Personality Item Pool (n.d.). IPIP home: a scientific collaboratory for the development of advanced measures of personality and other individual differences. [link](https://ipip.ori.org/)

title: Why did the stream change color? How researchers trace pollution upstream
excerpt: Rusty, green or brown water has a cause somewhere along the channel. Narrow down where the change begins with free maps and public water-quality data.
content:
"The stream behind my school changed color last summer." People notice it on the walk home: the water looks rusty for a few weeks, or turns green, or runs brown after a storm. Someone guesses at a cause, and that's where it ends.

Scientists ask one more question: where did the change come from? The first steps to answering it use free maps and public data that anyone can open.

## What a stream's color can and can't tell you

The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) notes that natural water always has some color. Soil runoff makes water yellow, red, brown or gray. Water rich in algae usually looks green. Tannins, dissolved substances from leaves, roots and plant remains, give water a yellow or brown tint that filtering probably would not remove.

Orange often has a natural cause too. The University of Connecticut's environmental health and safety office says orange slime in streams is often iron-oxidizing bacteria, which oxidize iron dissolved in groundwater in a reaction similar to rusting. The office says they aren't harmful and show that the stream is partly fed by groundwater. But mine drainage can turn water orange as well, as the Gold King example below shows.

![Glass jars and beakers of water and sediment on a wooden shelf, in shades from clear to greenish, brown and nearly black](/editorial/ideas/stream-color-pollution-research-idea/1.jpg "Water can look clear, green, brown or dark depending on what is in it, which is why color starts a question instead of answering it.")

What matters is what's in the water now that wasn't there before, and where it got in. Water flows one way, so every change has a location along the channel. In that sense, the water carries its own history.

## Walk upstream and find where it changes

One way to find a source is to compare the water upstream and downstream. The volunteer stream monitoring manual of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) suggests it for checking whether a suspected source has an impact.

First, pick a measurement that responds to what you suspect, such as conductivity. It measures how easily water carries an electric current, and it rises with dissolved salts and metals such as iron and aluminum. EPA notes that each stream tends to stay within a fairly steady range, so a significant change can point to a discharge.

Next, measure above an inflow, such as a side creek or a drain pipe, and below it. If the reading changes only below, that inflow becomes a suspect. Repeat at the next inflow upstream until you find the stretch where the change begins. EPA's manual also asks whether each site is far enough below drains and side streams. Two waters can flow side by side for a while before they mix.

![Drone view of a muddy brown channel meeting a dark gray rocky river beside green terraced fields, with a sharp line where the two waters meet](/editorial/ideas/stream-color-pollution-research-idea/2.jpg "Where two channels meet, the waters can stay separate for a while, so a reading below an inflow has to be taken far enough downstream.")

Two cautions apply. One reading proves little, because rain, season and time of day all shift water chemistry, so researchers repeat measurements. And a change doesn't always mean a pipe: groundwater seeping in can change readings too.

## What the Gold King Mine spill showed

On August 5, 2015, an EPA field investigation at the Gold King Mine near Silverton, Colorado, accidentally triggered the release of about 3 million gallons of acidic mine water into Cement Creek, a tributary of the Animas River. For days a bright yellow plume moved downstream, and some news reports called the Animas orange. EPA later explained the color: iron and aluminum from the mine water reacted with the river water.

The source was known on day one, because EPA's own work had caused the release. The harder question was where the metals went. In a January 2017 report, EPA scientists estimated that about 490,000 kg (close to 540 tons) of metals, mostly iron and aluminum, entered the Animas during the nine-hour release. Only about 1 percent came from inside the mine; the other 99 percent was scoured from a waste pile on the hillside and the bed of Cement Creek. The plume traveled about 550 km (342 miles) in nine days, from Colorado through New Mexico to Lake Powell in Utah. The team analyzed 1,758 water samples and 963 sediment samples from 294 sites, collected by EPA, states and tribes over the following year.

One limit is common in pollution research: the river already carried metals from hundreds of old and abandoned mines in the region. EPA notes that the spill's deposits, though bright yellow, held metal concentrations on average similar to those already stored in the riverbed. Separating one event from a long history of mining pollution is hard, even with thousands of samples.

## Tracing your own stream with free maps and data

The four steps below use free tools and public data. The whole project takes four to six weeks of part-time work, including the write-up.

**1. Trace your stream on free maps (1 to 2 hours).** Open [Google Earth](https://earth.google.com/web/) in your browser and follow your stream upstream in satellite view. Its [Measure tool](https://support.google.com/earth/answer/9010337?co=GENIE.Platform%3DDesktop) lets you click points along the channel and read off the length. This works for streams in Korea too. In the US, [USGS StreamStats](https://streamstats.usgs.gov/ss/) outlines the land area that drains to a point you pick on a stream, though what it offers varies by state.

**2. List everything that drains in (an afternoon, plus one walk).** Mark every side creek, pipe, ditch, farm and factory along your stretch. EPA's [watershed survey guide](https://archive.epa.gov/water/archive/web/html/vms31.html) suggests starting with maps and land use, then checking which industries hold permits to discharge into the stream. In the US, EPA's [How's My Waterway](https://mywaterway.epa.gov/) shows permitted dischargers for a location. Then check your map on a walk along public paths and bridges with a friend or an adult. Don't wade in or touch water that looks or smells like chemical or mine waste. Tell an adult and report it instead.

**3. Download public water-quality data (2 to 4 hours).** In the US, the [Water Quality Portal](https://www.waterqualitydata.us/) combines publicly available water-quality data from USGS, EPA and more than 400 state, federal, tribal and local agencies. You can search by county or by a radius around a point, choose measurements such as pH or specific conductance (the portal's name for conductivity), and download a CSV or Excel file. For USGS data added after March 11, 2024, use the portal's [beta version](https://www.waterqualitydata.us/beta/). In Korea, the [Water Environment Information System](https://water.nier.go.kr/), from the National Institute of Environmental Research, maps monitoring sites on rivers and lakes and lets you download readings such as BOD (how much oxygen microbes use to break down organic matter), total nitrogen, total phosphorus and dissolved oxygen as CSV files. The site is in Korean.

**4. Compare upstream and downstream readings (1 to 2 weeks of evenings).** In a free spreadsheet such as Google Sheets, plot one measurement against distance downstream and draw a vertical line wherever an inflow from step 2 joins. Compare readings from the same dates where you can. A clear jump or drop just after one of those lines is a lead worth following.

![A laptop on an orange table showing a topographic map of a town with a river winding across one corner, with a handheld GPS unit beside it](/editorial/ideas/stream-color-pollution-research-idea/3.jpg "Much of this project happens on a computer: mapping the stream, marking inflows and lining up monitoring sites.")

Scale is the main limit. Public monitoring sites are often kilometers apart and sampled weekly or monthly, and a small stream may have no site at all, so you may need to study the river it flows into. You can narrow down where a change happens between two sites, but you can't prove which pipe caused it. To add your own readings on a small stream, a low-cost pH color kit or a conductivity meter will do. Get your school's approval for the fieldwork first and follow [EPA's safety rules](https://archive.epa.gov/water/archive/web/html/vms23.html): never sample alone, never wade in swift or high water, wear gloves where you suspect pollution, and wash your hands afterward.

You'll finish with a map of numbered inflows and sites, a chart of readings by distance, and a poster or a 6 to 10 page paper on where the change appears and what might explain it.

## Stream questions with one measurement each

Here are three, each next to a version that's too big:

| Too big | Workable |
| --- | --- |
| Is the river in my city polluted? | Between the monitoring sites just above and below my city, how much does total phosphorus change, and is the change larger in the rainy season? |
| What turned the stream behind my school orange? | Over six visits, do pH and conductivity differ between the orange stretch of my stream and a stretch 200 m upstream, and does the orange begin at a groundwater seep? |
| How did the Gold King spill damage the Animas River? | In [EPA's posted sampling data](https://www.epa.gov/goldkingmine/emergency-response-monitoring-data-gold-king-mine-incident) from August 2015, how did dissolved iron change from the upper sites to the lower sites as the plume moved downstream? |

You can answer each workable version within a few weeks. If your answer turns out to be "we could not tell," that's still a finding, as long as you can explain why.

## Two other kinds of stream paper

The inflow map and the chart of readings give you a paper built on monitoring data. A literature review builds one from published studies, and a research proposal from a study you plan in full but don't run. A review might ask, for example, how researchers tell a natural iron seep from mine drainage when both turn a stream orange, and which measurements they rely on. Look in [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/) and the [USGS Publications Warehouse](https://pubs.usgs.gov/), where many U.S. Geological Survey studies are free to download. A proposal could plan the bigger version: a year of conductivity loggers above and below every inflow, with monthly lab tests for dissolved iron and aluminum. Include the question, the method, the data (logger readings, lab results, rainfall records) and who has to agree: the agency that manages the stream and the landowners, plus an ethics board if you also interview neighbors about when the color first appeared.

## From a walk home to a dataset

Research like this starts with a map and the stream you already walk past. Your stream was the question. Now research it.

Through CRI, students research with professors in many fields, such as biology, economics, chemistry and history, and turn a question of their own into a paper they write themselves, be it original research, a literature review or a research proposal. [CRI's research programs](/research) explain how it works.
