title: Why can a worm regrow its body? Stem cell research in a free online atlas
excerpt: A planarian worm can rebuild its body from a small piece. Follow one of its stem cell genes, piwi-1, from worm to human in free public databases.
content:
"I broke my arm. It took months to heal." Anyone who has spent weeks in a cast knows that slow wait. Your arm did heal, though, and the bone joined back together. But your body can't grow back a whole arm once it's gone. A small flatworm called a planarian can do something close to that. Remove its head, its tail or nearly any other part, and it grows the missing piece back.

So why can a worm regrow its body, and we can't? Biologists have studied that for more than a century, and some of their data is now free to explore on a laptop.

## Cut a planarian apart and small pieces regrow

Planarians are soft, flat-bodied worms. The species in the studies below, *Schmidtea mediterranea*, lives in fresh water around the Mediterranean. In the late 1800s, the American scientist Thomas Hunt Morgan found that a piece as small as 1/279th of a planarian could grow into a whole new worm.

![A brown planarian flatworm with two small eyespots near its rounded head, seen from above on a black background](/editorial/ideas/planarian-worm-regeneration-research-idea/1.jpg "Schmidtea mediterranea, the planarian species behind the studies described here. Photo: Alejandro Sánchez Alvarado, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons")

The worm's trick is a kind of stem cell called the neoblast. A stem cell can divide and turn into other types of cells. According to the U.S. National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS), neoblasts make up 20 to 30 percent of a planarian's body. They're spread throughout the body, so a cut in most places leaves some behind to rebuild what was lost.

Regrowth depends on these cells. When lab worms get a dose of radiation that kills their dividing cells, they can no longer regenerate. So the popular line "every piece grows into a new worm" goes too far. A piece needs living neoblasts in it.

We have stem cells too, but ours are specialists. As the Whitehead Institute explains, humans have blood stem cells in the bone marrow, skin stem cells and gut stem cells, each renewing its own tissue. In humans, only embryonic stem cells and germ cells (the cells that become eggs and sperm) are pluripotent, meaning able to make every cell type in the body. The planarian keeps adult cells that can do this. That's one big difference, though not the whole answer to why we can't regrow an arm.

## How regeneration researchers find the cells and read their genes

In the lab, regeneration research usually runs in two steps. First, find the cells that do the rebuilding. Then, read which genes are switched on inside them.

To find the cells, researchers use marker genes. A marker is a gene active in one cell type and not in most others, so staining for it makes those cells stand out under a microscope. For neoblasts, the standard marker is *piwi-1*, which older papers call *smedwi-1*. Its protein belongs to the PIWI family, a group defined by a fruit fly protein called PIWI.

To read the genes, labs use single-cell RNA sequencing, which shows the active genes in each cell. In 2018, Christopher Fincher, Peter Reddien and colleagues at the Whitehead Institute and MIT published data on 66,783 planarian cells in *Science*, covering essentially every cell type in the worm. They made the atlas public as a website, Planarian Digiworm.

A third tool, RNA interference (RNAi), shuts down one gene at a time to test whether it's needed. Shutting down *smedwi-2*, a gene related to *piwi-1*, blocks regeneration even though the neoblasts are still present (Reddien and colleagues, 2005).

## One stem cell rebuilt a worm: the 2011 study

A direct test of what a single neoblast can do came in 2011, from Daniel Wagner, Irving Wang and Peter Reddien at the Whitehead Institute, published in *Science*.

The team gave host worms a dose of radiation strong enough to kill their own neoblasts. Such worms can't regenerate, and in this study they died after about six weeks. Into each host, they injected a single cell from another planarian strain. They sorted the donor's cells by size and shape and picked ones that looked like clonogenic neoblasts (cNeoblasts), a type that can divide into a large colony.

In 7 of 130 transplanted worms, that one cell took over. These worms lived past seven weeks, grew new tissue where their bodies had been breaking down, regenerated eyespots and a feeding tube, and were eating again by eight weeks. The team grew three of the rescued worms into new lines and checked their DNA. It matched the donor strain, not the host: the descendants of one cell had replaced the host's tissues. The authors concluded that adult pluripotent stem cells, spread throughout the body, are the source of planarian regeneration.

![Bright cyan cells with branching edges on a dark navy background, seen through a microscope](/editorial/ideas/planarian-worm-regeneration-research-idea/2.jpg "The 2011 team picked donor cells about 10 micrometers (0.01 mm) across, far too small to see without a microscope. This stock image shows other cells, not planarian neoblasts.")

The limits: the rescue worked in only about 5 percent of transplanted worms, and it shows what one planarian cell can do inside a planarian, not what human cells could do.

## Follow piwi-1 from worm to human, no lab needed

You don't need worms or a lab for a first project. This one uses only public data, so there's nobody to recruit and no animals to keep. Plan on two to four weeks of after-school time.

**Step 1. Pick one gene: piwi-1 (about 1 hour).** Read the Whitehead Institute news story on the 2011 study, then the abstract of the 2005 paper that identified *smedwi-1* and *smedwi-2*. Write down every name the gene goes by. In the protein database UniProt, the worm protein is entry [Q2Q5Y9](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q2Q5Y9/entry), "Piwi-like protein 1", also listed as SMEDWI-1.

**Step 2. Open the free planarian cell atlas (1 to 2 hours).** Go to [Planarian Digiworm](https://digiworm.wi.mit.edu/) and open the Atlas tab. Type *piwi* into the search box and press Search. One result is the contig dd_Smed_v4_659_0_1, labeled "PIWI-like protein 1 (wi-1)". A contig is a pieced-together stretch of gene sequence; here it stands for the gene. Click that row, and the site draws a map in which each dot is one cell, colored from blue (gene barely active) to red (strongly active).

**Step 3. See which cells use it (2 to 3 hours).** Compare the colored map with the numbered cluster map beneath it. The site also lists where the gene is enriched: for *piwi-1*, the main clustering names only Neoblast clusters. A table of genes enriched in each cluster puts *piwi-1* near the top of the Neoblast list. Then click "PIWI-like protein 2 (wi-2)", the *smedwi-2* gene, and check whether its map matches. Save screenshots and record cluster names in a spreadsheet.

![Person seen from behind typing on a laptop that shows charts, with glasses and a phone on a white desk](/editorial/ideas/planarian-worm-regeneration-research-idea/3.jpg "Every step of this project runs in a web browser on free public databases.")

**Step 4. Find its human match (1 to 2 hours).** Open [NCBI BLAST](https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi), the free sequence-comparison tool of the U.S. National Center for Biotechnology Information. Choose Protein BLAST, enter Q2Q5Y9 in the query box, set the organism to *Homo sapiens*, and run it. BLAST lists human proteins whose sequence resembles the worm protein, each with an E-value: the smaller it is, the less likely the match is due to chance. Look for human PIWI proteins among the hits. UniProt puts the worm protein and human PIWIL1 in the same Piwi subfamily, and Digiworm's notes for this gene name PIWIL1 as its closest human match, so you can check your result. Then look up each hit in NCBI Gene. For human [PIWIL1](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/9271), the summary says the protein may help germline stem cells (which make eggs and sperm) and blood-forming stem cells renew themselves.

Be honest about what this step shows. A strong sequence match suggests two genes share an evolutionary origin. It doesn't mean the human gene does the same job in the same kind of cell.

**The finished project.** A short paper of four to six pages, or a one-page poster: the atlas maps for *piwi-1* and *wi-2* as Figure 1 (credit Fincher and colleagues, 2018), a table of the top human BLAST matches with their E-values as Table 1, and a discussion of what the comparison can and can't tell you.

## Regeneration questions a browser can answer

The workable versions are sized for Digiworm, BLAST and NCBI Gene:

| Too big | Workable |
| --- | --- |
| Why can't humans regrow an arm? | In the Digiworm atlas, which cell clusters show *piwi-1* activity, and does *wi-2* show the same pattern? |
| Could planarian genes help people heal? | Which human proteins are the closest BLAST matches to planarian PIWI-1, and what does NCBI Gene report about each one? |
| What lets planarians regenerate? | Of the top 25 genes in the atlas's Neoblast list, which ones does the atlas match to a human gene, and what does NCBI Gene say those human genes do? |

The left column would keep a lab busy for years. Each question on the right fits free tools and a few weeks.

Mapping *piwi-1* in the atlas gives you one kind of paper. A literature review or a research proposal makes an equally complete one. A literature review sets published studies side by side. One question: how have researchers tested which neoblasts can rebuild a whole worm (radiation, single-cell transplants, cell sorting, single-cell sequencing), and where do their findings disagree? Molinaro and Pearson's 2018 paper, in the Sources, is such a review. For the studies themselves, use [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) and [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/). A research proposal can plan an experiment that belongs in a university lab: say, whether zebrafish, which regrow lost fin tissue, switch on their PIWI genes in the regrowing fin. It sets out the method (trim the tail fins of anesthetized fish, then stain the regrowing tissue for PIWI gene activity 3, 7 and 14 days later), how many fish you'd sample at each point, and the approval you'd need: zebrafish are vertebrates, so a university animal care committee must approve the plan first.

Your broken arm was the question. Now research it.

At CRI, high school students work with university professors and teaching assistants on a question of their own and write their own paper, which may take the form of original research, a literature review or a research proposal. For this subject, Aziz Aboobaker, Professor of Comparative and Functional Genomics at the University of Oxford, leads [The Secrets of Immortality: Stem Cells, Gene Networks, and the Science of Regeneration](/research/program/cmttsli5900008ks3u8tdt94v). It is part of CRI's [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter), which meets online from December 19 to 30, 2026. Up to 5 students can join, and applications close December 15.

title: Does Instagram's ranked feed keep you scrolling? A high school phone study
excerpt: Instagram ranks your Home feed, but its Following feed shows posts in time order. Here's how to test whether the switch changes your daily minutes.
content:
"I can't stop scrolling, even when I'm bored." It usually comes out as a complaint about willpower. You can also read it as a question about design. The posts aren't that interesting, yet your thumb keeps moving. What is the feed doing to your attention, and is there a part of it you could measure yourself?

## Your feed is ranked, not in time order

Boredom should make you put the phone down. When it doesn't, one reasonable suspect is the order of the posts, which on Instagram is chosen for you.

In a 2023 explainer signed by Adam Mosseri, Instagram said the feed uses thousands of signals, such as posts you've liked, shared, saved or commented on, and roughly a dozen predictions. The five it looks at most closely are how likely you are to spend a few seconds on a post, comment on it, like it, share it, and tap on the profile photo. Meta's own page on the feed, updated in June 2026, also lists a prediction of how likely the first post you see is to keep you spending time in your feed during that session. So the next post is picked because the system guesses it will hold you, not because it's the newest one.

![Gold, silver and bronze medals numbered 1, 2 and 3 standing on white podium blocks against a lilac background](/editorial/ideas/instagram-ranked-feed-scrolling-research/1.jpg "A ranked feed is ordered like a podium: by predicted interest, not by the time each post was shared.")

Since March 2022, Instagram has also offered a Following view that shows posts from accounts you follow in reverse chronological order (newest first). The same Meta page says you reach it by tapping the Instagram logo on the app's home screen and choosing Following, and that it shows no recommended content. When the option launched, TechCrunch reported that it couldn't be set as the default. The app opens on the ranked feed, and you have to pick Following yourself.

That gives you two versions of the same app, which is what an experiment needs. They differ in two ways: the order of posts, and the suggested posts from accounts you don't follow, which Following leaves out. Say so in your write-up. Screen time also measures minutes, not attention. Minutes are a fair place to start, because your phone already records them.

## An experiment with one switch

Researchers test a question like this with an experiment. It changes one thing, called the independent variable (here, which feed you use), keeps everything else as similar as possible, and measures an outcome, called the dependent variable (here, minutes in the app each day).

![Two dark smartphones lying face down side by side, seen edge-on against a bright yellow background](/editorial/ideas/instagram-ranked-feed-scrolling-research/2.jpg "Two phones side by side stand in for the two weeks of your study: same app, same person, a different feed.")

You could compare two groups of people, one on each feed, or the same people in two periods, once on each feed. The second design suits a student project, because each person is compared with themselves. Its weakness is that the two periods can differ in other ways, such as an exam week, so plan for that.

## A 2023 Science study that switched feeds to time order

In July 2023, a team led by Andrew Guess (Princeton University), Neil Malhotra and Jennifer Pan (both Stanford University) published a study in *Science* as part of the US 2020 Facebook and Instagram Election Study, a project run by academic researchers together with Meta. For three months during the 2020 US election, they moved consenting US users from the default ranked feeds to reverse-chronological feeds and compared them with users who kept the default.

Moving users off the ranked feed substantially decreased the time they spent on Facebook and Instagram, and how active they were there. Time order didn't make everything better, though. On both platforms, those users saw more political content and more content from untrustworthy sources. Over the three months, the change didn't significantly shift their political attitudes or knowledge.

Keep its limits in mind: it studied US users during an unusual election season, and it measured time on the platforms, not attention. It can't tell you what happens to students at your school today, and that gap is where your own study fits.

## A two-week test on your own phone

If you plan to enter a science fair that follows [ISEF rules](https://www.societyforscience.org/isef/international-rules/human-participants/), get approval before Step 1: those rules count even a study of yourself as research with human participants, and an IRB (a board that reviews studies with people) must approve it first.

**Step 1: Record a normal week (7 days, about 2 minutes a day).** Turn on [Screen Time](https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/set-up-screen-time-for-yourself-iphbfa595995/ios) on an iPhone (Settings, then Screen Time) or [Digital Wellbeing](https://support.google.com/android/answer/9346420?hl=en) on Android (Settings, then Digital Wellbeing, then tap the chart; menu names vary by phone). Both show minutes per app. iPhone also counts pickups, and Android counts how often you unlock the phone and open apps. Make a [Google Sheet](https://www.google.com/sheets/about/) with one row per day and columns for Instagram minutes, total phone minutes, YouTube and TikTok minutes, and pickups or opens. Each morning, copy yesterday's totals, so late-night scrolling counts. iPhone lets you swipe back to past days; if your Android phone shows only today, copy the numbers just before you sleep instead. Use Instagram as you normally would.

Other apps matter: if your Instagram minutes drop later, the time may simply move elsewhere, and total phone time will show it.

**Step 2: Open the Following feed every time (7 days).** Since the app opens on the ranked feed, switch each time: tap the Instagram logo, then Following. Check your version of the app first. Meta notes that its options "may not be available to everyone," and Instagram's 2023 explainer said Following showed the last 30 days of posts, so notice whether you run out of new posts. Instagram ranks Reels and Explore separately, and your phone counts the whole app, so decide in advance whether you'll use Reels as usual in both weeks. Keep a tally of the times you forgot to switch.

**Step 3: Add classmates, with school approval (a few weeks for approval, then 2 to 3 weeks of data).** One person's two weeks is a case study; 10 to 20 people make a small dataset. Ask a teacher to help with school approval first. Under ISEF rules, the IRB must approve before you recruit anyone, and participants under 18 need their own agreement plus written permission from a parent. Show parents the form when you ask. Collect only numbers, through a [Google Form](https://www.google.com/forms/about/) with code names, not real names, account names or screenshots. Anyone can stop at any time. To handle the exam-week problem, flip a coin for each person: heads start with Following, tails with the ranked feed.

**Step 4: Compare minutes, ranked vs. Following (an afternoon, then a week to write).** For each person, find the average daily Instagram minutes in each week, then the difference. A chart with one pair of bars per person shows the pattern. To check whether the difference could be chance, Google Sheets has a paired t-test: `=T.TEST(ranked_range, following_range, 2, 1)`, where 2 means a two-tailed test and the final 1 means paired data ([how T.TEST works](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6055837?hl=en)). With 10 to 20 people, call it a pilot study. For background on smartphone use in Korea, the [Internet Addiction Prevention Center](https://www.iapc.or.kr/mediaView.do?idx=28&article_id=ICCART_0000000113163&type=A1) (also called Smart Shim Center), run by Korea's National Information Society Agency (NIA), offers the 2024 and 2025 national Smartphone Overdependence Survey reports as free PDFs (in Korean), with statistical tables you can cite in your introduction.

![Close-up of a printed blue bar chart with a blue pencil and a few coins resting on the page](/editorial/ideas/instagram-ranked-feed-scrolling-research/3.jpg "Your own chart needs only one pair of bars per person: the ranked week next to the Following week.")

The finished product is a one-page poster (question, method, chart, limits) or a short paper of four to six pages.

## Picking one number to track

"Social media" is a topic. In a hands-on test, a research question names who, what you change, and what you measure:

| Too big | Workable |
| --- | --- |
| Is the Instagram algorithm making teenagers addicted? | Do 10 to 20 students at my school spend fewer minutes a day on Instagram in a Following week than in a ranked week? |
| Does social media ruin attention? | When students use the Following feed, do the minutes they save on Instagram show up on YouTube or TikTok instead? |
| Why do people keep swiping when they're bored? | Do students open Instagram, or pick up their phones, fewer times a day in the Following week? |

The questions on the left are too big for one study. The ones on the right name one change and one number, and you can report the result after two weeks, whichever way it comes out.

Logging your own minutes is one kind of research, called original research. This topic also fits a literature review or a research proposal.

A **literature review** compares studies that already exist. The *Science* study found a time-ordered feed cut time on both platforms. How far do other feed experiments back that up, and did they count minutes from phone logs, platform records or people's own estimates? Search [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/) for "chronological feed" and [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) for "adolescent screen time".

A **research proposal** designs a study too big for one school. Would a semester on the Following feed change students' sleep, not only their minutes? The design might assign a few hundred students at several schools at random to one feed or the other, collecting screen-time logs and a sleep diary each morning. Then spell out the approvals: the school's permission, an IRB review, and a parent's permission plus the student's own agreement for anyone under 18.

## A small result still counts

If minutes drop in your two-week test, you have evidence that the feed you use matters for your group. If they don't, that's worth reporting too, and your limits section can say why.

Your scrolling was the question. Now research it.

If the part that interests you most is the default, the ranked feed the app opens on, you're asking how choices are designed. David McMillon, Assistant Professor of Economics at Emory University, teaches [The Architecture of Choice: Behavioral Economics, Cognitive Bias, and Nudge Theory](/research/program/cmttspe8800028ks31sr4a4cr) in CRI's [Winter Online Research Program](/research/winter): online, December 19 to 30, 2026, up to 5 students, applications close December 15. Each student there writes their own paper, and original research, literature reviews and research proposals are all welcome.

title: Rebuilding a war story no one wrote down: a high school research idea
excerpt: When a grandparent never talks about the war, the story isn't gone. Learn how to collect the pieces, check them against archives and find a research question.
content:
"My grandfather never talks about the war." Many families have someone like that, and maybe yours does too. You ask a question at dinner, and he changes the subject. Every time. After a while you stop asking, and the story starts to feel lost forever.

Usually it isn't lost. It's in pieces: a photo in a drawer, a letter, a place name he mentioned once, a date on an old document. Historians have a method for exactly this, and you can use it too.

## What a family silence means to a historian

Official war records mostly track armies, units and government decisions, not what one ordinary person went through. Much of that was never written down, so the people who lived it are often the only source.

Historians collect those memories through oral history: recording a person's spoken account of the past as a historical source. The Oral History Association, a professional body for people who do this work, notes that oral history relies on memory, so what people recall is filtered through the way their lives and surroundings have changed.

So an interview isn't the final answer. It's one source, and you check it like any other. You can ask what happened, and also how the story changed over time, or why parts of it were never told.

![A bundle of old envelopes tied with twine, an open handwritten letter in blue ink and a faded snapshot on a table](/editorial/ideas/family-war-story-oral-history-research/1.jpg "A story that was never told in full often survives as separate pieces, and each one can be checked.")

## How historians check a remembered story

The work has two parts. First, collect every piece you can find: interviews, photos, letters, diaries and official documents. Then cross-check them, which historians call corroboration: test each claim against a second, independent source.

In practice, break a story into small claims. "He was drafted in the spring" is a claim with a date. "His unit was near the river" is a claim with a place. For each one, look for an independent record and mark it as a match, a conflict, or "no record found." The Oral History Association's best practices ask interviewers to verify information presented as fact when possible and to place each account in its historical context.

A conflict isn't a failure. Say a family story places someone in a city in a month when a published timeline shows the front line was somewhere else. Now you've got something to explain. The date may have shifted in memory, two events may have merged into one, or the record may be incomplete. Working out which one it was is your research.

![A magnifying glass resting on a yellowed, handwritten log sheet marked 'Date' and 'Remarks', on top of a pale blue printed map](/editorial/ideas/family-war-story-oral-history-research/2.jpg "Dated records like logs and letters give you something fixed to compare a remembered story against.")

## One archive that collects these pieces

One large example is the Library of Congress's [Veterans History Project](https://www.loc.gov/vets/), created by Congress in 2000. According to the Library of Congress Magazine (January to February 2026), it now includes more than 121,000 collections of recorded interviews, original photographs, letters, diaries and unpublished memoirs from U.S. veterans. Volunteers, families and community members gather the material.

If your family is Korean, part of this archive covers your country's war. In 2015, the Library's [Folklife Today blog](https://blogs.loc.gov/folklife/2015/07/picturing-the-korean-war/) reported more than 12,000 collections related to the Korean War, 2,000 of them digitized. One belongs to Robert L. Barber, a private first class in the 1st Marine Division who wrote home to his mother. The blog dates one letter December 8, 1950, and calls that day "the start of the Battle of Chosin Reservoir." The Marine Corps' official history puts the main Chinese attack on the night of November 27 to 28 and treats December 8 as the start of the final stage. Even a trusted source is worth cross-checking.

The archive has clear limits. It was built for the stories of U.S. veterans, so a Korean grandparent's story usually doesn't belong there. It holds what people chose to record and donate, so it isn't a random sample of everyone who served. It preserves the pieces, but the cross-checking is the researcher's job. The count also keeps growing, so treat 121,000 as a snapshot from early 2026.

## How to try it with your own family

Allow six to eight weeks of part-time work.

**1. Interview family, with school approval (one to two weeks once approved).** A chat at dinner needs nobody's permission. Recording a relative's memories for a project you'll share is different, because it's research with a person. Tell a teacher first and get your school's approval. Ask whether your school, or any competition you plan to enter, requires an ethics review (an IRB, or institutional review board). Explain the project to your relative, get their informed consent, and ask them to sign a simple release form. The [Veterans History Project field kit](https://www.loc.gov/programs/veterans-history-project/how-to-participate/vhp-field-kit/) shows what such forms and question lists look like. If you also interview anyone under 18, such as a cousin, you'll need a parent's consent as well.

War memories can be painful. The Oral History Association says narrators have the right to refuse to discuss certain subjects, so tell your relative they can skip any question or stop at any time. Start with life before the war, or with one photo. Record on your phone, then type it up with [oTranscribe](https://otranscribe.com/), a free web tool that keeps your audio on your computer. It works on desktop computers only, and you do the typing yourself, so allow several hours per hour of audio.

![Overhead view of an older man's arm and a younger person's hands holding an open family photo album on a dark table, with two empty mugs nearby](/editorial/ideas/family-war-story-oral-history-research/3.jpg "Looking through an album together, one photo at a time, can be an easier start than a direct question about the war.")

**2. Scan old photos and letters (one or two afternoons).** Google's [PhotoScan](https://www.google.com/photos/scan/) app combines several shots of a print to remove glare and corrects the angle. Scan the back of each photo too, because names and dates are often written there. Give every item a number and log it in a spreadsheet: what it is, any date or place on it, and who keeps the original. Then give the originals back.

**3. Match dates to public archives (one to two weeks).** List every date, place and unit name from your interviews and documents. For a Korean family, start with these three public sources, all in Korean.

- The National Archives of Korea's [Korean War (6·25) records site](https://theme.archives.go.kr/next/625/intro.do) introduces 934 records, such as government documents, operation orders and photos, and offers copies of those that can be made public. Its timeline lists major national events, such as the January 4, 1951 retreat from Seoul, not one person's movements.
- The National Institute of Korean History's [Archives of Korean History](https://archive.history.go.kr) has an oral history section with recorded accounts of people and events in modern Korean history. Some items can be viewed online, and others only at the Institute in Gwacheon.
- The War Memorial of Korea's [Korean War Archives](https://www.koreanwar.or.kr/) lets you browse photos, maps and oral history videos by year, place and people. Some items can only be seen at its archive center in Yongsan, Seoul, open since November 2022.

For a U.S. veteran, look for Veterans History Project collections from the same war and check their descriptions for the same unit. Then turn your matched dates into a timeline with [TimelineJS](https://timeline.knightlab.com/), an open-source tool from Knight Lab that reads a Google Sheet. The sheet must be published to the web, so leave out anything your relative hasn't agreed to share.

**4. Note where the stories disagree (a few days).** Make a table with one row per claim: what your family says, what the record says, whether they match, and possible reasons if they don't. If two relatives tell the same event differently, add both versions. A difference doesn't mean someone is lying. Time, retelling and the parts a family chose to pass on all shape a memory.

By the end you'll have a timeline, that comparison table and a short paper of about 6 to 10 pages, or a poster, explaining what matched, what conflicted and what's still unknown. Before you share it, show it to the relative you interviewed: the Oral History Association recommends giving narrators a chance to approve an oral history before it's made public.

## Shrinking "what was the war like?"

Historians have written whole books on "What was the war like?" Your question should use a small set of sources and something you can compare.

| Too big | Workable |
| --- | --- |
| What was the Korean War like? | How closely do the dates in one relative's account match major events on the National Archives of Korea war timeline? |
| Why do veterans stay silent about war? | In 10 digitized Korean War interviews from the Veterans History Project, which topics do veterans describe at length, and which do they pass over quickly? |
| How did the war change Korean families? | How do two generations of one family tell the same wartime event, and where do their versions differ? |

The second question uses only public recordings. The first and third depend on interviews, so the approval and consent steps above apply.

Family stories also lend themselves to two other kinds of paper. A **literature review** draws its answer from studies already in print. Take oral historians of the Korean War: how do they handle a memory that clashes with the written record? Do they correct it, print both versions, or study the gap itself? Search [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/) and [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/), which archives many history journals.

A **research proposal** takes the study beyond one family. Scale up the third question: how does one war story change as it passes from survivors to their children and grandchildren? You'd plan interviews with three generations in 20 families, then log and compare every claim. You'd need about 60 recordings, their transcripts and matching archive records. Before the first interview, an IRB would need to approve it, every narrator would sign a consent form, and a parent would consent for any grandchild under 18.

Your family's silence was the question. Now research it.

History is one of many fields CRI students work in, along with biology, economics and chemistry. Each student researches with a professor and writes a paper on a question of their own, which might be original research, a literature review or a research proposal. To see how that works, explore [CRI's research programs](/research).
